title: Ngôn Ngữ Của Nhà Lãnh Đạo (The Language of Leaders, Vietnamese edition)
author: Kevin Murray
summary:
The Language of Leaders makes a single central argument: that communication is not a soft support function of leadership but the core mechanism through which leadership actually happens. Kevin Murray, a former journalist who spent years as a communications advisor to chief executives, builds the book around interviews and case material from dozens of senior leaders across large organizations, using their own accounts to show how the words, stories, and listening habits of a leader directly shape whether employees trust, follow, and go beyond minimum effort for them. His recurring claim is that most leaders drastically underestimate how much of their real influence runs through communication rather than through formal authority or strategic insight.

The book works through the practical mechanics of leadership communication in roughly the order a leader would need to master them: clarifying what you actually stand for and want to say, learning to say it with authenticity rather than borrowed corporate language, building narrative and storytelling skill so messages stick and travel, and developing genuine two-way listening rather than one-directional broadcasting. Murray is particularly insistent that authenticity cannot be faked at scale — that employees are highly sensitive to the gap between a leader's stated values and their visible behavior, and that this gap, more than any single communication failure, is what destroys trust over time.

A second major thread concerns communication during high-stakes moments: change programs, crises, mergers, and periods of uncertainty, when the volume and clarity of leadership communication matters most and is hardest to sustain. Murray argues that leaders often go quiet exactly when employees need them to be most visible and most honest, out of an understandable but counterproductive instinct to wait until they have complete information. He uses case examples to show that admitting uncertainty candidly, on a regular cadence, builds more trust than infrequent, overly polished statements that turn out to be wrong or incomplete.

The book closes by tying communication skill back to results, arguing that engagement, retention, and even financial performance correlate with how well leaders communicate — not as a nice-to-have cultural benefit but as a measurable driver of organizational outcomes. Throughout, Murray resists reducing leadership communication to media training or rhetorical technique, insisting instead that the words leaders use are only as credible as the character and consistency behind them, and that developing "the language of leaders" is inseparable from the harder work of clarifying what a leader genuinely believes and is willing to be held accountable for.

sections.title: Why Communication Is Central to Leadership
sections.summary: This opening chapter makes the book's foundational case: that leadership is, at its core, an act of persuasion and meaning-making carried out through language, not a separate skill layered on top of strategic or operational competence. Murray draws on interviews with senior executives to argue that the leaders who are remembered as exceptional are disproportionately the ones who could articulate a clear, compelling sense of purpose that others could repeat and act on themselves. The chapter pushes back directly on the idea that communication is a delegable function handled by a comms department, arguing instead that no spokesperson can substitute for a leader's own voice on matters that define the organization's direction. It sets up the rest of the book by promising a practical breakdown of what leaders who communicate well actually do differently.
keyLessons: Communication is framed as inseparable from leadership itself, not a supporting skill leaders can outsource.
The clarity and repeatability of a leader's stated purpose is treated as a measurable leadership asset.
No communications team can substitute for the leader's own credible voice on matters of real consequence.

sections.title: Finding Your Own Voice
sections.summary: Murray argues that many leaders default to generic, corporate-sounding language precisely because it feels safe, and that this safety comes at the direct cost of credibility and memorability. The chapter works through exercises and examples aimed at helping leaders identify what they actually believe and want to say, distinct from what sounds appropriately leader-like, arguing that authenticity is detectable by employees even when it can't be precisely articulated by them. He uses contrasting examples of leaders who spoke in borrowed, abstract language against those who spoke plainly and specifically, showing the latter consistently landing with more impact. The chapter closes by connecting authentic voice to the next requirement — the discipline of having something genuinely worth saying, not just a distinctive way of saying it.
keyLessons: Generic corporate language is presented as a common but costly default that undermines trust rather than protecting the speaker.
Authenticity is something employees detect intuitively, even when they can't articulate exactly what feels off about inauthentic messaging.
Finding your voice is treated as a discipline of clarifying belief first, not primarily a stylistic exercise.

sections.title: Building a Compelling Story
sections.summary: This chapter shifts from voice to structure, arguing that leaders who communicate memorably tend to think in narrative — a clear beginning, tension, and resolution — rather than in lists of priorities or abstract values statements. Murray draws on storytelling craft to show how specific, concrete detail (a real customer, a real moment of difficulty) makes strategic messages travel through an organization in a way that bullet points never do. He includes case examples of leaders who successfully reframed difficult strategic pivots as a coherent story employees could retell in their own words, arguing that this retellability is the real test of whether a message has landed. The chapter transitions into the practicalities of what leaders should actually say, having established how they should shape it.
keyLessons: Narrative structure, not bullet-point clarity alone, is what makes strategic messages memorable and repeatable.
Concrete, specific detail outperforms abstract values language for making a message stick.
Whether employees can retell a message in their own words is offered as a practical test of communication success.

sections.title: What Leaders Need to Say
sections.summary: Here Murray gets specific about content: a compelling purpose, a clear strategic direction, honest acknowledgment of challenges, and recognition of people's contributions are treated as the recurring core content leaders need to communicate regardless of industry or context. He argues that many leaders over-invest in communicating strategy and under-invest in communicating purpose and recognition, leaving employees with a clear sense of what the organization is doing but a weak sense of why it matters or whether their work is seen. The chapter includes practical guidance on balancing consistency (saying the same core things repeatedly) against staleness, arguing repetition is far less risky than leaders assume. It hands off into the chapter on listening, since Murray argues content quality depends on hearing what the organization actually needs to hear addressed.
keyLessons: Purpose and recognition are identified as commonly under-communicated relative to strategy and priorities.
Leaders tend to underestimate how much repetition is needed before a message actually sinks in organization-wide.
Communication content should be shaped by what the audience needs addressed, not only by what the leader wants to announce.

sections.title: The Discipline of Listening
sections.summary: Murray argues that the leaders who are perceived as the best communicators are, counterintuitively, often the best listeners — because genuine two-way engagement is what makes people trust that a leader's messages reflect real understanding rather than a scripted agenda. The chapter details practical listening mechanisms leaders can build into their routines: structured skip-level conversations, deliberately unfiltered feedback channels, and visible responsiveness to what's heard, arguing that listening without visible follow-through is worse than not asking at all. He warns specifically against the trap of surrounding yourself with people who tell you what you want to hear, describing this as one of the most common and damaging failure modes among senior leaders. The chapter transitions into crisis and change communication, where the cost of poor listening becomes most visible and immediate.
keyLessons: Strong listening habits, not just strong speaking skills, are treated as core to being perceived as a trustworthy communicator.
Listening without visible follow-through is described as more damaging to trust than not soliciting input at all.
Senior leaders are specifically warned about the risk of being filtered off from unfiltered feedback as they rise.

sections.title: Communicating Through Change and Crisis
sections.summary: This chapter addresses the highest-stakes application of leadership communication: periods of restructuring, crisis, or major uncertainty, when Murray argues leaders most often go quiet at exactly the moment employees need visible, honest communication most. He makes the case that regular, candid updates — including honest admissions of what is not yet known — build more trust over the course of a crisis than infrequent, overly polished statements that later prove incomplete or wrong. Case material in this chapter focuses on leaders who maintained a steady communication cadence through difficult transitions versus those who withdrew, with the former group consistently retaining more organizational trust and engagement afterward. The chapter closes by connecting communication behavior during hard periods directly to the leader's long-term credibility, transitioning into the book's final argument about measurable business impact.
keyLessons: Leaders tend to withdraw communication exactly when employees need it most, which Murray identifies as a critical and correctable failure pattern.
Regular candid updates, including honest uncertainty, build more durable trust than polished but infrequent statements.
Communication behavior during a single crisis period can define a leader's credibility for years afterward.

sections.title: The Business Case for Better Communication
sections.summary: The closing chapter ties everything back to organizational performance, arguing that engagement, retention, and execution speed are measurably linked to how well leaders communicate, and presenting this as a business case rather than a soft cultural argument for investing in leadership communication skill. Murray summarizes the book's practical throughline — authentic voice, disciplined content, genuine listening, and consistency under pressure — as a coherent skill set that can be deliberately developed rather than treated as an innate trait some leaders simply have. The chapter ends by returning to the book's opening claim, arguing that leaders who treat communication as central to the job, rather than peripheral to it, consistently outperform those who treat it as a delegable function.
keyLessons: Communication quality is presented as measurably linked to engagement and retention, not only to leader popularity.
The book's four practical pillars — voice, content, listening, and consistency under pressure — are framed as a learnable skill set.
The closing argument reasserts that treating communication as core to leadership, not peripheral, is itself a performance decision.
Communication is the mechanism through which leadership actually happens, not a support function that can be delegated to a communications team.
Employees detect the gap between a leader's stated values and their visible behavior faster than leaders assume, and that gap is what erodes trust.
Authentic, plain, specific language consistently outperforms generic corporate phrasing for building trust and memorability.
Concrete narrative and specific detail make strategic messages travel through an organization far better than lists or values statements.
Purpose and recognition are commonly under-communicated relative to strategy — both need deliberate, repeated attention.
Listening only builds trust when it is followed by visible responsiveness; listening without follow-through is worse than not asking.
Leaders should increase, not decrease, communication frequency during crisis and change, even when full information isn't yet available.
Repetition of core messages is far less risky than most leaders assume, and is usually necessary before a message actually sticks.

quotes.text: Leadership and communication are inseparable — you cannot lead if you cannot communicate, and how you communicate defines what kind of leader you are.
quotes.attribution: Kevin Murray, The Language of Leaders

quotes.text: Employees forgive a great deal, but they do not forgive a leader who says one thing and does another.
quotes.attribution: Kevin Murray, The Language of Leaders

quotes.text: People don't remember bullet points. They remember stories they can retell.
quotes.attribution: Kevin Murray, The Language of Leaders

quotes.text: The most dangerous position for a leader is to be surrounded by people who only tell them what they want to hear.
quotes.attribution: Kevin Murray, The Language of Leaders

whoThisIsFor: Executives, senior managers, and rising leaders who want a practical framework for how they talk to and listen to the people they lead, rather than a book on public speaking technique.
whenToReadThis: Especially useful when stepping into a more senior leadership role, or heading into a period of organizational change, restructuring, or uncertainty where communication cadence matters most.

authorBio.name: Kevin Murray
authorBio.bio:
Kevin Murray is a British communications expert who built his career first as a broadcast journalist before moving into corporate communications advisory work, eventually serving as an advisor and coach to chief executives and senior leadership teams across major organizations. He has held leadership roles within the communications and public relations industry, including presidency of a major professional communications body in the UK.

His work draws on decades of direct, close-in advisory access to senior executives navigating leadership transitions, crises, and major strategic communication challenges, which forms much of the case material underpinning his writing and speaking. He continues to work as a speaker, coach, and advisor on executive communication.

conceptsFrameworks.name: The Authenticity Gap
conceptsFrameworks.definition: Murray's term for the space between what a leader says they value and what employees actually observe them doing, which he argues is the single largest driver of whether leadership communication is trusted or dismissed.

conceptsFrameworks.name: The Retellability Test
conceptsFrameworks.definition: A practical standard Murray proposes for judging whether a leadership message has actually landed: whether employees can retell it accurately and in their own words to a colleague, rather than merely being able to recite it back.

conceptsFrameworks.name: Communicating Through the Fog
conceptsFrameworks.definition: Murray's framing for crisis and change communication, describing the practice of giving regular, honest updates — including open acknowledgment of what is not yet known — rather than waiting for full clarity before speaking.

actionSteps: Write down your organization's or team's current strategic priority in plain, specific language with no corporate jargon, then read it aloud and cut anything that sounds like it could apply to any company.
Turn your next strategic update into a short narrative with a concrete before/tension/after structure rather than a bulleted list of priorities.
Set up one structured, unfiltered listening mechanism this month — a skip-level conversation or open feedback channel — and commit publicly to acting visibly on at least one thing you hear.
Identify one area of current uncertainty you've been avoiding discussing publicly, and give a short, honest update on it even though you don't have a full answer yet.
Audit the ratio of strategy-focused versus purpose- and recognition-focused communication you've sent in the last month, and rebalance if it's skewed heavily toward strategy.
reflectionQuestions: Where is there currently a gap between what you say you value and what your team actually sees you do?
Which recent message of yours would your team struggle to retell accurately in their own words — and why?
When was the last time you changed a decision or plan visibly because of something you heard from an employee, and did they know it was because of them?

points: The book relies heavily on interview-based case studies of senior leaders describing their own communication practices in retrospect, which is a self-reported and somewhat self-flattering evidence base rather than independently observed or measured behavior.

Because the case material is drawn mainly from large, well-resourced corporations, the practical advice — dedicated listening mechanisms, communications support, structured crisis cadences — assumes a level of organizational infrastructure that may not transfer cleanly to small businesses or resource-constrained leaders.

The book's claim that better communication measurably drives engagement and performance is directionally well-supported by broader organizational research, but the specific causal weight Murray assigns to communication skill versus other factors (compensation, job design, market conditions) is asserted more than rigorously isolated within the book itself.

As with much leadership-communication literature, the framework risks becoming a checklist of techniques (storytelling, listening rituals) that can be performed without the underlying authenticity the book insists is the actual active ingredient.
criticalTake.contextNote: The book's core argument — that communication behavior, especially during uncertainty, has measurable effects on trust and retention — has been reinforced rather than undermined by subsequent research and practice on remote and hybrid-era leadership communication, where visible, frequent, honest updates have become even more central to organizational trust.
